prompt: Why is an IP address a weak rate-limit key on its own?

options.text: IPv6 addresses are too long to use as efficient Redis counter keys
Many users share one IP, and attackers can rotate through many IPs
A client's IP changes on almost every request, so counts never add up
Load balancers replace every client IP with their own, hiding them all

explanation: Shared NATs and corporate proxies put many users behind one IP (too strict), while attackers rotate through many IPs (too loose). Key length isn't a real problem, client IPs don't change per request, and proxies pass the original IP in headers like X-Forwarded-For.

prompt: A token bucket has B = 10 and R = 2/s and is full. A client sends 15 requests at once. How many succeed?
explanation: The bucket holds 10 tokens; the other 5 are rejected until it refills.

prompt: Which algorithm is being exploited, and what fixes it?
scenario: Your API allows 100 requests per minute using per-minute counters. A scraper sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, every minute.

options.text: Token bucket letting a full burst through; switch to a leaky bucket
Fixed window boundary burst; use a sliding window counter or log
Sliding log missing old timestamps; switch to a fixed window counter
Nothing is exploited; 100 per minute is exactly what each window allows

explanation: Per-minute counters reset at the boundary, so 100 at 12:00:59 plus 100 at 12:01:00 gets 2x the limit through in a second. Sliding windows look back a full window from now. This isn't a token bucket or sliding log, switching to fixed windows is the cause not the fix, and 200 in two seconds is not the intended rate.

prompt: Limit 100/min, previous window 80 requests, current 30, 25% into the current window. Sliding window counter estimate?
Which algorithm smooths output to a perfectly steady rate at the cost of added delay?

options.text: Token bucket
Fixed window
Leaky bucket
Sliding window counter

explanation: A leaky bucket is a queue drained at a fixed rate. The others reject rather than queue.

prompt: Why is the sliding window log memory-heavy?

options.text: It stores a timestamp for every request inside the window
It stores each full request body so requests can be replayed
It needs a dedicated Redis server for every user it tracks
It keeps every timestamp forever and never trims old entries

explanation: A sliding log keeps one timestamp per request in the window, so memory grows with limit x active users. It doesn't store bodies, doesn't need per-user servers, and trims entries older than the window.

scenario: Each app server runs `count = GET key; if count < 100: SET key count+1`. Under load, clients regularly get 104 or 105 requests through per minute.

options.text: Redis is too slow under load, so counter updates arrive after the check
Two servers read the same count before either writes; use atomic INCR
The one-minute window is too short, so counts reset before they settle
The load balancer duplicates some requests, so each one is counted twice

explanation: It's a read-then-write race: two servers GET 99, both allow, both SET 100. Atomic INCR (or a Lua script for multi-step logic) fixes it. Redis speed and window length don't cause overshoot, and duplicated requests would be counted, not let through extra.

prompt: How many requests a minute can one client really make?
scenario: You have 10 app servers behind a round-robin load balancer. Each server keeps its own in-memory limit of 100 requests per minute per user.

options.text: Unlimited

explanation: Ten servers × 100 each, with the load balancer spreading the client's requests.

prompt: Your Redis rate-limit store is down. Which are reasonable choices? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fail open for normal API limits
Fail closed for login-attempt limits
Silently crash the app servers
Fall back to approximate local limits

explanation: Fail open protects availability, fail closed protects security, local fallbacks give rough protection. Crashing (c) is never the plan.

prompt: Where should a '10 exports per day' limit live?

options.text: At the CDN edge, so abusive export calls are blocked before origin
Inside the export service, which knows what counts as an export
At the API gateway as a generic per-user requests-per-day limit
In the client app, which can disable the button after ten exports

explanation: Business-specific limits need business context, so they belong in the export service. The CDN and a generic gateway limit see requests, not exports (and would count retries or status polls), and client-only limits are trivially bypassed.

prompt: What should a rate-limited request receive?

options.text: 503 Service Unavailable, since the server is refusing extra load
429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header
200 OK with an empty body so clients don't treat it as an error
A silently dropped connection so abusers learn nothing at all

explanation: 429 tells the client exactly what happened and Retry-After tells it when to try again. 503 signals the whole service is down (and invites generic retries), a 200 hides the failure, and a dropped connection looks like a network fault and triggers blind retries.

prompt: Why add jitter to client retries?

options.text: To slow every retry down so clients give up instead of retrying
So rejected clients don't all retry at once and recreate the spike
Because HTTP requires a random delay before resending a request
To spread retries across different keys and slip past the limiter

explanation: Without jitter, clients rejected together back off by the same amount and retry together, recreating the spike. Jitter isn't meant to make clients give up, HTTP doesn't require it, and it doesn't change which key is counted.
